draft.title: Cost-benefit analysis
card: Cost-benefit analysis is a way to judge an option. List all the costs and all the benefits of it, including ones that fall on other people.
Where possible, put a dollar value on each item. Some items, such as a quieter street, are hard to value, so they may be described in words instead.
Add up the benefits and the costs, then compare them. If the benefits outweigh the costs, the option is worth taking.
If the costs outweigh the benefits, the option is not worth taking as it stands. Another option may do better.
draft.remember: List every cost and benefit, value what you can, then compare the totals.

a.q: What is the main purpose of a cost-benefit analysis?
opts: To weigh the total benefits of an option against its costs
To find the option with the lowest cost, whatever the benefits
To find the option with the top benefits, whatever the costs
To record how much money a business spent on an option
a.why: A cost-benefit analysis weighs benefits against costs to judge whether an option is worth taking. Looking at costs alone or benefits alone is tempting, but it ignores half of the comparison.
a.clue: Both sides of the list matter.

b.q: A council in Bendigo plans a skate park. It estimates benefits of $3 million in health and fun for users. Costs are $2 million to build plus $0.4 million in noise costs to nearby homes. What should the analysis conclude?
opts: Benefits of $3m outweigh costs of $2.4m, so build it
Benefits of $3m outweigh the $2m build cost, so build it
Costs of $2.4m are close to benefits, so do not build it
The noise cannot be valued, so no analysis is possible
b.why: The costs include the build cost and the noise cost to neighbours, a total of $2.4 million. Benefits of $3 million are higher, so the park is worth building. Leaving out the noise cost is tempting, but the analysis lists all costs, including those on other people.
b.clue: Add every cost, including those on neighbours.
